title: The students returning to school after sexual assault: ‘You go back the next day, and you just deal with it’
text:
In the wake of the latest headlines about alleged sexual assaults involving school boys and the death of a 16-year-old girl from suspected sexual choking, national cabinet has agreed to prioritise its plan to end sexual violence against women, the NSW government has flagged a new set of priorities with education ministers and the federal government has announced draft legislation for a digital duty of care. Meanwhile, the victim at the centre of an alleged gang-rape involving two students from a Sydney private school and another boy has prepared to sit her HSC exams.
“I can’t imagine what she is going through,” police prosecutor Sergeant Rhonda Riley told the court last month. “But she will need to complete her HSC going through pain and fear – not only mentally – for some time going forward.”
As peer-on-peer violence continues to rise, many girls, who make up the majority of school-age sexual assault victims, have no choice but to return to school to continue their education in the shadow of their assault. And in many cases, they must continue to share a campus with their assailant.
“In previous generations, it was more common for child sexual abuse to be inflicted by an adult than an adolescent,” reports the 2023 Australian Child Maltreatment Study. “In contemporary Australia, it is more common for child sexual abuse to be inflicted by an adolescent than an adult.”
These findings are echoed by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, and frontline services are buckling under the weight of a spike in peer-on-peer violence. While experts agree that this mounting crisis can’t be tackled by education institutions alone, schools make up a vital component of the conversation.
In 2024, the federal government began the welcome rollout of $77.6m in funding for the delivery of age-appropriate consent and respectful relationships education programs in schools across the country. But a growing cohort of advocates and experts are warning that as students become more informed as a result of education around consent, many of those same institutions are ill-equipped to deal with the fallout.
Facing an abuser on school grounds
Anna Coutts-Trotter has lost count of the stories she has heard from girls who feel their school failed them.
As a social worker, survivor and the founder of the Survivor Hub, a national organisation that holds meet-ups for sexual assault survivors of all ages and their families, 25-year-old Coutts-Trotter says she hears stories of schools not intervening, mishandling a report, or of female students having to keep attending the same school – facing their abuser regularly on the school grounds “many, many times”.
“Where there’s been no other option for moving the survivor to another school,” she says. “And also the person who’s used violence not being expelled or suspended because of no other option.”
“I hear that all the time,” she says.
In the event of a sexual assault being reported to schools, the education department guidelines vary from state to state. A school’s response intersects with a number of overlapping considerations, including criminal law, the school’s obligations under mandatory reporting, the institution’s broader duties of care to their students, and their disciplinary powers. And while incidents between peers offsite can hugely affect the education and wellbeing of students on campus, in some states, schools are limited to only offering discipline or recourse to incidents that happen on their grounds.
“We have scenarios where principals can be empowered to act but only where misconduct or assault took place on campus or on a school-related activity,” says Prof Michael Salter, the director of Childlight UNSW, the Australasian hub of the global research institute seeking to prevent child sexual abuse and exploitation. “But if an assault has taken place in a private house, on a Friday night … those kids will show up to school on the Monday, and the school may not have any powers to address what took place on the Friday.”
‘Teachers just have to sort something out’
Dani Villafaña experienced sexual assault when she was 14 by a peer from another school who she met through an extracurricular activity. She confided in her school counsellor, who, because of mandatory reporting guidelines, then had to tell the police.
“I gave a police interview, and that was a really distressing and traumatic experience in and of itself,” says Villafaña, who founded the advocacy group Youth Against Sexual Violence. “But in my case, and as is the case with most reports, charges were not followed through.
“The system we have now is: if a report has been made but it hasn’t reached that threshold of criminality … you go back to school the next day, and you just deal with it, and the teachers just have to sort something out.”
Salter agrees. “Schools’ responses are very much shaped by their mandatory reporting obligations, rather than necessarily the welfare of a student who’s been harmed, or the student who may be accused of having harmed,” he says.
“If schools are not empowered or able to respond in an appropriate way to an incident of sexual misconduct, and yet they are delivering respectful relationships and consent education, there would seem to be an obvious contradiction, or even hypocrisy,” Salter says.
In Villafaña’s case, her school responded well, she says. They organised for her to see a specialist counsellor on school grounds, in school hours, offered additional learning supports in class to help with PTSD symptoms, and facilitated conversations with her parents around what had happened. “I was really lucky,” she says. “My school’s internal response was one that was guided by care and compassion.”
Villafaña published research earlier this year on best practice for responding to peer-to-peer sexual assault within schools, as part of a Churchill fellowship. It found that without this support, girls will often disengage from class or may be left to manage their timetable so they aren’t in the same places as their perpetrators. Eventually, many stop going altogether.
The research also highlights that schools have a duty of care to perpetrators. “One of the hard things to grapple with is that young people, regardless of if they’ve experienced harm or if they’ve caused harm, need support to continue to engage with education,” Villafaña says.
She says calls to expel the accused private school boys in Sydney are misguided – because they will probably just end up in the public system, which has even fewer resources to deal with them. She believes perpetrators need to be moved away from victims, but with their own support structures in place.
‘They’re not being protected’
But is it reasonable or even realistic to expect schools to support and care for both victims and the accused when already overworked staff are not necessarily trained or equipped to handle these disclosures?
Yes, says Salter. “As long as there is reasonable and practical guidance and advice given to schools,” he adds. “South Australia, for example, has quite complex guidance … and the principles that it’s based on are quite public and transparent.”
To counteract this state lottery that high school students are subjected to, Villafaña has teamed up with End Rape on Campus Australia founder Sharna Bremner and advocacy group Fair Agenda to launch a campaign for a national code of conduct. Based on the existing university model announced earlier this year, the code would be extended to secondary schools to ensure that they are guided by a minimum set of standards for educators.
“The next step is to ensure that systematic responses to sexual misconduct and assault in schools are prioritising student welfare, safety and educational continuity. This goes beyond school curricula and culture,” agrees Salter. “We need deconfliction and coordination of police investigation, child protection, mandatory reporting and school discipline responses, and a commitment to upholding the rights of all children impacted when an allegation of sexual abuse or misconduct is made in an educational environment.”
Instead, “we’re relying on the discernment of individual school leaders,” Villafaña says.
Leaders who often fumble their response. Coutts-Trotter remembers one particular survivor from a regional school in New South Wales who was forced to sit in assembly as school leaders raised the matter of her assault in front of the whole school.
“We’re talking about children, we’re talking about 12- to 17-year-olds,” she says. “And they’re not being protected; they’re not safe.”
